I find that for difficult or complex issues it helps to discuss a simpler, easier to relate to narrative, then break the initial issue down and compare the narrative to the original issue. This has the effect of disarming the other party - rather than immediately commencing an anger / passion filled argument, you lower the tensions of both parties, build up a history and have the ability to discuss the original issue in an informative way.

Consider dogs. 1000's of years ago, we didn't have dogs. We had wolves. And they attacked us - brutally. In the wild, at night, killing us, our children. Until one day some smart dude left food out for the wolves at night, and he got lucky and some smart wolf started catching on - that if he didnt kill the man, the man would feed him. And the wolf had pups, and the man had kids, and they each passed along that knowledge, for generations, until the wolves and men were comfortable with each other. Then the humans started leaving fires for warmth and roofs for shelter for the wolves out at night. Until the wolves began to trust the humans. The wolves didn't have to hunt for food anymore. The humans fed them. The humans warmed them. The humans sheltered them. So it was in those wolves best interest to protect the humans. They were loyal to those humans. They loved them. Generations later, they were now dogs. And now when a wild pack of wolves or coyotes came in the night, the dogs fought to protected their humans.

This is what we've done with vaccines. We've taken a wild an dangerous disease (wolf) that used to kill us, and through science and time, we have 'trained' it to protect us, to be loyal to us. So when the wolves come, our dogs (vaccines) are there to protect us.
